problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before authorization, at up to 15,000 transactions per second during seasonal peaks. Fraud patterns change within weeks, confirmed chargeback labels arrive days to weeks later, and auditors may ask months later why a score was produced. Seven ML staff work with operations and no dedicated ML platform team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

points.description: A model-specific service serves real-time predictions through distributed microservices, blocking clients until results are available; streaming data is processed in real time using shared stores for raw data and features. A scheduled MLOps orchestrator performs batch training, versions data, deploys multiple model versions, and tracks production behavior, with humans adjusting models when needed. Trade-off: This supports continuous ingestion, controlled experimentation, and broad monitoring, but shared stores lack feature-specific guarantees and manual adjustment slows response. Multiple production versions and real-time serving also increase operational complexity and resource needs.

Each model runs as its own service, while features are persisted in general-purpose data stores. Streaming inputs are processed in real time and sent to a distributed model-serving microservice, whose prediction request blocks the client until a result is returned. Trade-off: This provides continuously updated predictions with independently deployable model services and straightforward storage choices. It gives up some operational simplicity and may increase latency or coupling because clients wait synchronously and the stores lack specialized feature-management support.

The system keeps ML data in a shared data store and stores features there without specialized feature-store support. A dedicated data-version repository records dataset or feature revisions, while production monitoring tracks model usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness. Trade-off: This gains shared access, reproducibility, and broad production visibility, but generic feature storage gives up specialized feature-management capabilities and may require more application-level coordination; versioning and comprehensive monitoring also add operational and storage overhead.

An MLOps system uses an orchestrator to run scheduled, batch-based training pipelines and manage versioned data. It deploys multiple model versions concurrently, while humans review monitoring results and manually adjust and redeploy models as needed. Trade-off: This provides reproducible data management, regular automation, and safer version comparison, but concurrent deployments and manual adjustment increase operational complexity and slow responses to model-quality changes. Scheduled batch retraining may also miss rapid changes between runs.

Each model runs as its own service, retrieving features from a feature store. Streaming data is processed in real time and sent to distributed model-serving microservices; clients block until each prediction or score is available. Trade-off: This provides continuously updated features and low-latency, synchronous predictions with independently deployable models. It gives up client responsiveness while waiting, and incurs the operational complexity of coordinating streaming ingestion, real-time processing, feature storage, and multiple services.

An ML orchestrator runs scheduled batch-training pipelines using versioned data, then deploys multiple model versions concurrently. Monitoring can automatically adjust models or initiate corrective pipeline actions while MLOps coordinates delivery and lifecycle management. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, repeatable operations, and safer comparison or rollout of model versions, but increases orchestration and deployment complexity, consumes resources for parallel versions, and may leave models unchanged between scheduled runs unless monitoring triggers intervention.

A continuous data stream is processed in real time, with features stored in general-purpose data stores. Each model runs as its own service, exposing a local API that clients call synchronously and block on until predictions are returned. Trade-off: This supports continuously updated features and promptly available predictions with clear model-service boundaries. It gives up client responsiveness during model latency and may require additional work to achieve low-latency, consistent feature access from stores lacking specialized support.

An MLOps system uses an orchestrator to run batch training pipelines when new data becomes available, with data versions stored in a dedicated repository. It deploys multiple model versions concurrently and relies on human review of monitoring results to adjust and redeploy models. Trade-off: This supports reproducibility, automated retraining, and comparison or fallback across versions, but manual adjustment slows responses to degradation and increases operational effort. Concurrent production versions also increase deployment and monitoring complexity.

adrs.title: Build the authorization-time scoring path around live activity
adrs.context: Each authorization needs a score using recent card activity, with a 30 ms p99 target at 15,000 transactions per second. The solution streams transactions, updates aggregates in real time and waits synchronously for an online model service.

options.name: Streamed features and synchronous model microservice
pros: Provides recent features and a synchronous score before authorization.
Matches the streaming input and real-time aggregate path.
cons: No p99 measurement demonstrates the 30 ms target.
General-purpose stores and synchronous calls may add latency and operational coordination.
options.reason: R1 calls for current activity and scoring before authorization. Q1 supports an online path, although it does not force a distributed service or generic feature store.

options.name: Use a feature store for the online aggregates
cons: The requirements do not call for feature-store-specific capabilities; operations would have another specialized component to run.
options.reason: The feature-store contrast supports the same requirements, so Redis-style generic storage is a free implementation choice.

options.name: Serve through a local service API
cons: The point does not provide evidence that its latency is better or worse for this workload.
options.reason: The local API contrast also fits R1; the stated requirements and available evidence do not force the microservice boundary.

adrs.title: Retain score and model provenance for audit
adrs.context: For 13 months, the team must be able to retrieve each score's model version and all inputs, together with the training data used to build that model.

options.name: Append-only score records and tracked training snapshots
pros: Retains the model version and every input value with the score.
Records the training-data snapshot and model artifact for each run.
cons: The design space values do not specify retention duration, immutable storage or retrieval time.
options.reason: R3 and Q3 force reconstructable per-score records and a link to training data. The specific on-premises object store and MLflow implementation are choices; the shared-store and data-version-repository values are approximate fits.
options.fit_note: The values abstract away the append-only table, 13-month retention, on-premises object storage and MLflow snapshot implementation.

adrs.title: Retrain on a schedule and review a shadow model
adrs.context: Confirmed fraud labels arrive late, so the system needs recurring retraining and a comparison against the current model before a candidate is promoted. Q4 limits the entire response to 48 hours after the segment's loss rate rises.

options.name: Nightly batch training with a three-day human-reviewed shadow
pros: Compares candidate and current behavior before human promotion.
Records training snapshots and model artifacts.
cons: The three-day shadow interval exceeds Q4's 48-hour limit.
options.reason: Nightly batch training addresses R2 and shadow comparison meets the review condition, but the solution does not meet Q4 because three days is longer than 48 hours. The space's multiple-versions value only approximately represents a shadow candidate, and manual adjustment only approximately represents promotion.
options.fit_note: Shadow execution is not the same as serving multiple production versions, and human promotion is not precisely model adjustment based on monitoring.

options.name: Trigger retraining when new training data arrives
pros: Can start a training run as soon as new data becomes available.
cons: Does not fix the three-day shadow review bottleneck.
options.reason: This trigger also fits R2, but the requirements do not force it over a nightly schedule; neither schedule can compensate for the stated review interval.

options.name: Automate model adjustment
pros: Could reduce delay from manual adjustment.
cons: The checked combination still retains the three-day shadow period and misses Q4.
options.reason: Q4 requires a faster end-to-end path, but it does not prescribe automatic promotion; the solution's manual choice is not forced.

uncovered.decision: Fall back to the existing rule engine when scoring or a data source fails, so authorization continues.
uncovered.solution_quote: If the call times out or fails, the switch uses the existing rule engine for that transaction and logs that no score was used.

uncovered.decision: Return the three strongest score-increasing features as a cardholder explanation.
uncovered.solution_quote: The service returns, with every score, the three features that pushed the score up the most, which the dispute team uses to explain declines to cardholders.

Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.
